Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Immunoinformatics based design and evaluation of a multi-epitope vaccine candidate targeting the envelopment polyprotein of Andes orthohantavirus.
papers.abstract: Andes Orthohantavirus is known to be the etiological agent for hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), which is a highly dangerous disease with a very high death rate. There is no vaccine available to date to protect against this disease. This project aimed to develop a multi-epitope vaccine for Andes Orthohantavirus using immunoinformatics. Epitopes of CTL, HTL, and B cell types were predicted for the shortlisted Glycoprotein precursor after testing antigenicity, allergenicity, toxicity, and subcellular location. The chosen epitopes were combined using appropriate linkers and β-defensin as an adjuvant to create a multi-epitope vaccine. The final vaccine construct had a length of 296 amino acids and showed excellent antigenicity (0.7297), non-allergenicity, structural stability, and solubility properties. The structure of the vaccine construct showed that 94.6% of residues lie in the preferred areas of the Ramachandran plot, thus ensuring good stereochemistry. Molecular docking and normal mode analysis results confirmed the stable binding of the vaccine construct to TLR-3 receptors. At the same time, immune simulation revealed a fast degradation of antigens, production of antibodies, memory B-cells, and cytokines. In silico cloning integrated the codon-optimized gene with a CAI value of 0.97 and a GC percentage of 49.77% into the plasmid vector pET-28a(+). The designed multi-epitope vaccine displayed good predicted immunogenicity, structure, and expression properties that made it suitable to be used as a potential vaccine candidate against Andes Orthohantavirus infection. Further experimental validation is needed to assess its safety and effectiveness.

analysis.background: Andes Orthohantavirus causes hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, a highly dangerous disease with very high death rate, and no vaccine is currently available.
analysis.methods: Immunoinformatics was used to predict CTL, HTL, and B‑cell epitopes from the glycoprotein precursor, filter them for antigenicity, allergenicity, toxicity, and subcellular location, link them with β‑defensin adjuvant, model the construct, dock it to TLR‑3, perform normal mode analysis, run immune simulations, and conduct in‑silico codon optimization (CAI 0.97, GC 49.77%).
analysis.results: The 296‑aa vaccine showed antigenicity 0.7297, non‑allergenicity, structural stability (94.6% residues in favored Ramachandran regions), stable binding to TLR‑3, simulated rapid antigen degradation, antibody production, memory B‑cell and cytokine responses, and favorable codon‑usage metrics.
analysis.contribution: The work presents a computationally designed multi‑epitope vaccine candidate with predicted immunogenicity, stability, and expression suitability against Andes Orthohantavirus infection.
analysis.limitations: Results are derived solely from in‑silico analyses presented in an abstract; experimental validation of safety and effectiveness is needed.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes orthohantavirus causes hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome with high mortality and no licensed vaccine. Methods: Immunoinformatics predicted CTL, HTL, and B‑cell epitopes from the glycoprotein precursor, filtered them for antigenicity, allergenicity, toxicity, and subcellular location, linked them with β‑defensin adjuvant, modeled the construct, docked to TLR‑3, performed normal mode analysis, immune simulation, and in‑silico codon optimization (CAI 0.97, GC 49.77%). Results: The 296‑aa construct showed antigenicity 0.7297, non‑allergenicity, structural stability (94.6% residues in favored Ramachandran regions), stable TLR‑3 binding, and simulated antibody, memory B‑cell, and cytokine responses. Contribution: Provides a computationally designed multi‑epitope vaccine candidate with favorable immunogenic and expression properties for Andes orthohantavirus. Limitations: Findings are based only on in‑silico data from an abstract; experimental validation is required.

analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒 正汉坦病毒 引起 汉坦病毒心肺综合征,这是一种致死率极高的高度危险疾病,且目前尚无疫苗可用。
analysis_zh.methods: 采用免疫信息学预测糖蛋白前体中的CTL、HTL和B细胞表位,依据抗原性、致敏性、毒性及亚细胞定位进行筛选,将其与β-防御素佐剂连接,构建模型并对接TLR-3,进行正规模式分析,开展免疫模拟,并进行体外密码子优化(CAI 0.97,GC 49.77%)。
analysis_zh.results: 该296氨基酸疫苗显示抗原性为0.7297,非致敏性,结构稳定(94.6%残基位于Ramachandran有利区),与TLR-3结合稳定,模拟显示抗原快速降解、抗体产生、记忆B细胞及细胞因子应答,并具备良好的密码子使用指标。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究提出了一种基于计算设计的多表位疫苗候选体,预测对安第斯病毒 正汉坦病毒 感染具有免疫原性、稳定性和表达适宜性。
analysis_zh.limitations: 结果仅来源于摘要中呈现的体外(in silico)分析,需进行实验验证以确认安全性和有效性。

papers.title: Strengthening readiness for emerging infectious diseases in Somalia through hantavirus preparedness
papers.abstract: Emerging infectious diseases continue to pose substantial threats to global public health security, with low- and middle-income countries bearing a disproportionate burden of vulnerability. In May 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Africa and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) convened a joint technical briefing (webinar) on hantavirus preparedness, underscoring the importance of proactive readiness for this and other zoonotic threats across the African continent. While no hantavirus outbreak and no direct evidence of human hantavirus circulation have been reported in Somalia, this briefing presents a timely opportunity to critically examine Somalia’s capacity to detect and respond to emerging infectious diseases more broadly. This commentary evaluates Somalia’s current public health infrastructure against the key preparedness domains highlighted in the WHO–Africa CDC briefing including surveillance, laboratory diagnostics, risk communication, and One Health coordination and identifies critical gaps that require urgent policy attention. Drawing on published evidence and international frameworks, we offer context-specific recommendations to strengthen Somalia’s health security architecture before a crisis emerges. Proactive investment in preparedness is both a moral imperative and a strategic necessity for a country at the intersection of complex humanitarian conditions and persistent epidemic risk.

Abstract Emerging infectious diseases continue to pose substantial threats to global public health security, with low- and middle-income countries bearing a disproportionate burden of vulnerability. In May 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Africa and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) convened a joint technical briefing (webinar) on hantavirus preparedness, underscoring the importance of proactive readiness for this and other zoonotic threats across the African continent. While no hantavirus outbreak and no direct evidence of human hantavirus circulation have been reported in Somalia, this briefing presents a timely opportunity to critically examine Somalia’s capacity to detect and respond to emerging infectious diseases more broadly. This commentary evaluates Somalia’s current public health infrastructure against the key preparedness domains highlighted in the WHO–Africa CDC briefing including surveillance, laboratory diagnostics, risk communication, and One Health coordination and identifies critical gaps that require urgent policy attention. Drawing on published evidence and international frameworks, we offer context-specific recommendations to strengthen Somalia’s health security architecture before a crisis emerges. Proactive investment in preparedness is both a moral imperative and a strategic necessity for a country at the intersection of complex humanitarian conditions and persistent epidemic risk. 1 Introduction Emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases represent one of the most consequential threats to global public health in the 21st century.Diseases of zoonotic origin those trans­ mitted from animals to humans account for approximately 60% of known human infec­ tious diseases androughly 75% of emerging pathogens identified over recent decades [1]. The COVID-19 pandemic, alongside recurrent outbreaks of Ebola, Marburg, and mpox, has exposed the catastrophic cost of inadequate preparedness, particularly in low-resource settings where health systemcapacity is structurally constrained [2].Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) face a dual challenge: they carry the highest bur­ den ofinfectious disease while simultaneously confronting the most severe deficits in the Page 2 of 8 Issack Discover Public Health (2026) 23:1840 systems required to detect and respond to emerging threats.Sub-Saharan Africa, and the Horn of Africa in particular, remains among the most vulnerable regions in the world to pandemic-scale events,owing to ecological conditions favorable to zoonotic spillover, high population density in informal settlements, limited diagnosticinfrastructure, and fragmented health governance [3].Against this backdrop, the joint technical briefing (webinar) convened by the WorldHealth Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Africa and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) in May 2026on hantavirus preparedness represents a significant institutional signal. Prompted by WHO and Africa CDC’s response to emerging hantaviruscases [4], the briefing was designed to strengthen proactive readiness across the region, encouraging member states across the Africancontinent to assess their surveillance systems, laboratory capacities, and One Health coordination mechanisms in anticipation of potentialzoonotic threats [5]. This forward-looking approach aligns with the principles embedded in the International Health Regulations (2005) andthe Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, both of which emphasize preparedness as the cornerstone of resilient health systems [6].This commentary uses the WHO–Africa CDC hantavirus technical briefing as an analytical lens through which to examine Somalia’spreparedness for emerging infectious diseases. We do not assert that Somalia faces an imminent hantavirus threat; rather, we argue that thepreparedness domains highlighted in the briefing surveillance, diagnostics, risk communication, and multisectoral coordination reflectuniversal gaps in Somalia’s health security infrastructure that merit urgent and sustained policy attention. 2 Why hantavirus preparedness matters globally and regionally Hantaviruses are RNA viruses belonging to the family Hantaviridae, transmitted to humans primarily through inhalation of aerosolscontaminated with the excreta of infected rodents [7]. They cause two serious clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome(HFRS), which is prevalent in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus car­ diopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), which predominates in the Americas. Casefatality rates range from less than 1% for some HFRS-causing strains to over 30% for certain HCPS-causing strains [7]. Critically, no licensedvaccine or specific antiviral treatment is currently available, making prevention, early detection, and supportive care the prin­ cipal public healthtools. The continued global relevance of hantavirus was underscored in May 2026, when WHO reported responding to human hantavirus caseslinked to a cruise ship [4].Evidence of hantavirus-seropositive rodents has been documented in multiple African countries, including in sub-Saharan Africa, raising the possibility, at a regional and ecological level, of undetected human cases on the continent [8]. Such rodentseroprevalence data indicate biological plausibility across parts of Africa; they are not, however, direct evidence of hantavirus circulation inany specific country, includ­ ing Somalia [8]. The widespread presence of reservoir rodent species (particularly Muri­ nae and Cricetidae),combined with limited diagnostic capacity to distinguish hantavirus from other febrile illnesses such as malaria, typhoid, leptospirosis, andviral hemorrhagic fevers, means that hantavirus infections in Africa may be significantly underdiagnosed and underreported [8].The globalpublic health community has increasingly recognized that the absence of confirmed cases does not imply the absence of risk lessons rein­ forcedby repeated experiences with emerging pathogens. The WHO–Africa CDC brief­ ing reflects this paradigm shift: preparedness must precededetection. For African health Page 3 of 8 Issack Discover Public Health (2026) 23:1840 systems, this requires investment in syndromic surveillance, rodent reservoir monitor­ ing, differential diagnosticcapacity, and cross-sectoral preparedness planning before an outbreak demands emergency mobilization. 3 Relevance to Somalia Somalia presents a complex and challenging public health environment shaped by three decades of conflict, recurrent humanitarian crises, andfragmented governance. Despite recent political stabilization efforts and incremental progress in health system recon­ struction, the FederalGovernment of Somalia’s capacity to prevent, detect, and respond to infectious disease outbreaks remains severely constrained [9]. Thecountry has one of the lowest health expenditure levels in the world, inadequate health workforce density, and a healthcare infrastructure thatwas severely disrupted during the civil conflict period and remains unevenly distributed across regions [10].Somalia’s epidemiological pro­ fileis dominated by endemic and epidemic-prone diseases, including cholera, measles, acute watery diarrhea, polio, and malaria. In 2022 and2023, the country simultaneously managed a severe drought-driven humanitarian emergency, widespread displacement of over 3.8 millioninternally displaced persons (IDPs), and multiple concurrent disease outbreaks [11]. The convergence of malnutrition, poor sanitation,overcrowded displace­ ment settlements, and limited access to healthcare creates conditions highly condu­ cive to infectious disease transmissionand amplification.While hantavirus has not been reported in Somalia, the ecological and socioeconomic conditions that favor zoonotic­ spillover are present. Rodent infestation is a recognized problem in IDP settlements and urban areas [12]. Human–animal interfaces arefrequent in a predominantly pastoralist society, and exposure to rodent reservoirs in agricultural and peri-urban environments is common.Crucially, the diagnostic tools and clinical awareness needed to identify hantavirus, or other emerging zoonotic diseases, remain very limitedwithin Somalia’s current health system capacity. It should be emphasized, however, that no direct evi­ dence of hantavirus circulation in Somaliacurrently exists; the concern is one of biologi­ cal plausibility and general preparedness rather than documented or imminent human risk. Inprinciple, an emerging infectious disease could circulate for a period before iden­ tification—the broad scenario that the WHO–Africa CDCbriefing urges countries to guard against. 4 Key messages from the WHO–Africa CDC technical briefing As a webinar, this briefing served as a timely prompt rather than a formally published technical document, and no recording or presentationmaterials from it are publicly available; the preparedness principles it reiterated are themselves established in verifi­ able international guidance, to which the messages below are anchored in particular the International Health Regulations (2005) [6], the One Health Joint Plan of Action [13], and established WHO and Africa CDC preparedness and surveillance frameworks [14,15]. 4.1 Surveillance systems and early warning The technical briefing emphasized the centrality of robust surveillance systems to early detection of emerging zoonotic threats. Effectivesurveillance requires functional dis­ ease reporting networks, standardized case definitions, real-time data management, and Page 4 of 8 Issack Discover Public Health (2026) 23:1840 integrationbetween human, animal, and environmental health surveillance streams [5]. Event-based surveillance—the systematic monitoring ofinformal reports and commu­ nity signals is particularly valuable in settings where laboratory-confirmed case identi­ fication is delayed. 4.2 Laboratory preparedness and diagnostics A core message of the briefing was that laboratory capacity for emerging pathogen diag­ nostics is foundational to preparedness. This includesaccess to biosafety level-2 and level-3 facilities, availability of validated diagnostic assays (including serological and molecular tests foremerging viruses), specimen referral networks, and quality-assured laboratory practices. Without these, even clinically suspicious casescannot be con­ firmed, hampering both outbreak response and epidemiological understanding [5]. 4.3 Risk communication and community engagement The briefing underlined that risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) are not supplementary but integral to preparedness.Effective RCCE enables commu­ nities to recognize and report unusual illness presentations, reduces harmful health- seeking delays, buildstrust between communities and health authorities, and counters misinformation. Importantly, RCCE must be culturally adapted andlinguistically acces­ sible to be effective in diverse community contexts [16]. 4.4 One Health preparedness and multisectoral coordination Perhaps the most structurally significant message of the briefing was its emphasis on One Health an integrative approach recognizing theinterdependence of human, ani­ mal, and environmental health. For zoonotic diseases such as hantavirus, preparedness requires activecoordination between ministries of health, livestock, environment, and agriculture; engagement with veterinary and wildlife authorities; andjoint surveillance and response planning [5, 13]. Siloed sectoral approaches are fundamentally insufficient for managing the complexdynamics of zoonotic disease emergence. 5 Preparedness gaps and risks in Somalia 5.1 Surveillance limitations Somalia’s disease surveillance infrastructure is fragmented and heavily dependent on external humanitarian partners for operationalcontinuity. The Integrated Disease Sur­ veillance and Response (IDSR) framework, endorsed by the African Union and WHO, has beenpartially implemented in Somalia but lacks consistent application across all federal member states [9]. Data completeness, timeliness ofreporting, and feedback mechanisms remain significant challenges. Syndromic surveillance for febrile hemor­ rhagic illness syndromesremains limited in functionality and geographic coverage, and is inconsistently implemented across federal member states, which isparticularly concern­ ing from an emerging disease preparedness standpoint. 5.2 Laboratory and diagnostic capacity Somalia’s disease surveillance infrastructure is fragmented and heavily dependent on external humanitarian partners for operationalcontinuity. The Integrated Disease Sur­ veillance and Response (IDSR) framework, endorsed by the African Union and WHO, Page 5 of 8 Issack Discover Public Health (2026) 23:1840 has beenpartially implemented in Somalia but lacks consistent application across all federal member states [9]. Data completeness, timeliness ofreporting, and feedback mechanisms remain significant challenges. Syndromic surveillance for febrile hemor­ rhagic illness syndromesremains limited in functionality and geographic coverage, and is inconsistently implemented across federal member states, which isparticularly concern­ ing from an emerging disease preparedness standpoint. 5.3 Cross-border health security challenges Somalia shares porous borders with Ethiopia, Kenya, and Djibouti, and significant cross- border movement occurs through pastoralistmigration, livestock trade, and refugee flows. These movement patterns facilitate rapid regional dissemination of infectious dis­ eases, asdemonstrated during cholera and measles outbreaks [11]. Health surveillance at points of entry is limited in coverage and functionality,particularly at land crossings used by pastoralist and informal cross-border movement, and this, together with weak cross-border informationsharing mechanisms, represents meaningful vulnerabilities in regional health security. 5.4 Humanitarian and displacement-related vulnerabilities As of 2023, Somalia hosts one of the largest internally displaced populations in sub- Saharan Africa [11]. IDP settlements are characterizedby overcrowding, inadequate sanitation, poor rodent vector control, and extremely limited access to healthcare. These conditions amplifyboth the risk of zoonotic exposure and the potential for rapid second­ ary transmission of person-to-person pathogens. Humanitarian crises alsodivert gov­ ernment and partner attention and resources away from preparedness activities toward acute response, creating cyclical gaps inreadiness. 5.5 Workforce and infrastructure constraints Somalia faces a severe shortage of trained public health professionals, epidemiologists, laboratory scientists, and infection control specialists.Health worker density is among the lowest globally, and much of the existing health workforce is concentrated in major urban centers,leaving significant coverage gaps in rural and peri-urban areas [10]. The capacity for rapid deployment of field epidemiology teams,outbreak investigation, and case management during novel disease events is correspondingly limited. 6 Policy and public health recommendations The recommendations below follow directly from the gaps identified in Sect.5and are grouped by feasibility. Immediate, feasible actions—achievable within existing part­ nerships and resources—include full operationalization of IDSR with community- and event-based surveillance(6.1, addressing 5.1), strengthened specimen-referral agree­ ments with regional and international reference laboratories (6.3, short-termcomponent, addressing 5.2), scaling Field Epidemiology Training Program cohorts (6.2, address­ ing 5.5), and preparedness-phase riskcommunication (6.6). Longer-term, resource- dependent goals include establishing in-country BSL-2 molecular diagnostic capacity (6.3,medium-term component, addressing 5.2), formalized One Health coordination structures (6.5), and institutionalized cross-border data-sharingand RISLNET participa­ tion (6.4, addressing 5.3). Abstract Emerging infectious diseases continue to pose substantial threats to global public health security, with low- and middle-income countries bearing a disproportionate burden of vulnerability. In May 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Africa and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) convened a joint technical briefing (webinar) on hantavirus preparedness, underscoring the importance of proactive readiness for this and other zoonotic threats across the African continent. While no hantavirus outbreak and no direct evidence of human hantavirus circulation have been reported in Somalia, this briefing presents a timely opportunity to critically examine Somalia’s capacity to detect and respond to emerging infectious diseases more broadly. This commentary evaluates Somalia’s current public health infrastructure against the key preparedness domains highlighted in the WHO–Africa CDC briefing including surveillance, laboratory diagnostics, risk communication, and One Health coordination and identifies critical gaps that require urgent policy attention. Drawing on published evidence and international frameworks, we offer context-specific recommendations to strengthen Somalia’s health security architecture before a crisis emerges. Proactive investment in preparedness is both a moral imperative and a strategic necessity for a country at the intersection of complex humanitarian conditions and persistent epidemic risk. 1 Introduction Emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases represent one of the most consequential threats to global public health in the 21st century.Diseases of zoonotic origin those trans­ mitted from animals to humans account for approximately 60% of known human infec­ tious diseases androughly 75% of emerging pathogens identified over recent decades [1]. The COVID-19 pandemic, alongside recurrent outbreaks of Ebola, Marburg, and mpox, has exposed the catastrophic cost of inadequate preparedness, particularly in low-resource settings where health systemcapacity is structurally constrained [2].Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) face a dual challenge: they carry the highest bur­ den ofinfectious disease while simultaneously confronting the most severe deficits in the Page 2 of 8 Issack Discover Public Health (2026) 23:1840 systems required to detect and respond to emerging threats.Sub-Saharan Africa, and the Horn of Africa in particular, remains among the most vulnerable regions in the world to pandemic-scale events,owing to ecological conditions favorable to zoonotic spillover, high population density in informal settlements, limited diagnosticinfrastructure, and fragmented health governance [3].Against this backdrop, the joint technical briefing (webinar) convened by the WorldHealth Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Africa and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) in May 2026on hantavirus preparedness represents a significant institutional signal. Prompted by WHO and Africa CDC’s response to emerging hantaviruscases [4], the briefing was designed to strengthen proactive readiness across the region, encouraging member states across the Africancontinent to assess their surveillance systems, laboratory capacities, and One Health coordination mechanisms in anticipation of potentialzoonotic threats [5]. This forward-looking approach aligns with the principles embedded in the International Health Regulations (2005) andthe Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, both of which emphasize preparedness as the cornerstone of resilient health systems [6].This commentary uses the WHO–Africa CDC hantavirus technical briefing as an analytical lens through which to examine Somalia’spreparedness for emerging infectious diseases. We do not assert that Somalia faces an imminent hantavirus threat; rather, we argue that thepreparedness domains highlighted in the briefing surveillance, diagnostics, risk communication, and multisectoral coordination reflectuniversal gaps in Somalia’s health security infrastructure that merit urgent and sustained policy attention. 2 Why hantavirus preparedness matters globally and regionally Hantaviruses are RNA viruses belonging to the family Hantaviridae, transmitted to humans primarily through inhalation of aerosolscontaminated with the excreta of infected rodents [7]. They cause two serious clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome(HFRS), which is prevalent in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus car­ diopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), which predominates in the Americas. Casefatality rates range from less than 1% for some HFRS-causing strains to over 30% for certain HCPS-causing strains [7]. Critically, no licensedvaccine or specific antiviral treatment is currently available, making prevention, early detection, and supportive care the prin­ cipal public healthtools. The continued global relevance of hantavirus was underscored in May 2026, when WHO reported responding to human hantavirus caseslinked to a cruise ship [4].Evidence of hantavirus-seropositive rodents has been documented in multiple African countries, including in sub-Saharan Africa, raising the possibility, at a regional and ecological level, of undetected human cases on the continent [8]. Such rodentseroprevalence data indicate biological plausibility across parts of Africa; they are not, however, direct evidence of hantavirus circulation inany specific country, includ­ ing Somalia [8]. The widespread presence of reservoir rodent species (particularly Muri­ nae and Cricetidae),combined with limited diagnostic capacity to distinguish hantavirus from other febrile illnesses such as malaria, typhoid, leptospirosis, andviral hemorrhagic fevers, means that hantavirus infections in Africa may be significantly underdiagnosed and underreported [8].The globalpublic health community has increasingly recognized that the absence of confirmed cases does not imply the absence of risk lessons rein­ forcedby repeated experiences with emerging pathogens. The WHO–Africa CDC brief­ ing reflects this paradigm shift: preparedness must precededetection. papers.title: Andes Virus Exposure and Nosocomial Transmission Events to Healthcare Personnel: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Andes virus (ANDV) is a high-consequence infectious disease with substantial mortality. On 2 May 2026, the World Health Organization reported a multinational ANDV outbreak, raising questions regarding the risk of transmission to healthcare personnel (HCP). METHODS: We performed a systematic review per PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO:CRD420261283806) for studies describing healthcare-associated ANDV exposure or transmission events to HCP. RESULTS: Eight studies reporting on 7 events were included, describing a total of 17 healthcare-associated cases. Overall, 207 individuals were exposed, including 118 HCP, resulting in 8 infections and 4 deaths among HCP. Studies describing HCP infections reported none or inadequate personal protective equipment (PPE) use. CONCLUSIONS: Transmission of ANDV to HCP has been reported in the setting of delayed implementation of transmission-based precautions or breaches in infection control practice. Limitations in published exposure events highlight the need for standardized reporting of exposure events and outcomes as well as infection prevention measures implemented.
papers.journal: Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America

analysis.background: ANDV is a high‑consequence pathogen with substantial mortality (A1) and a recent multinational outbreak raised concerns about HCP risk (A2).
analysis.main_directions: The review applied PRISMA methods to identify healthcare‑associated exposure events (A3), highlighted inadequate PPE use (A6), and linked transmission to delayed or breached infection‑control precautions (A7).
analysis.current_state: Eight studies describing seven events reported 17 healthcare‑associated cases (A4); among 207 exposed individuals, 8 HCP infections occurred with four deaths (A5), confirming that transmission occurs when precautions fail (A7).
analysis.gaps: Published reports are few and lack standardized exposure and outcome documentation, limiting inference (A8).
analysis.future_research: Standardized reporting of exposure events, systematic surveillance of HCP infections, and evaluation of infection‑prevention interventions are needed (A8).

analysis.summary_en: Background: ANDV is a high‑consequence virus with recent multinational outbreak raising HCP risk (A1, A2). Main directions: Systematic review identified healthcare‑associated exposure events, noted inadequate PPE and breaches in infection control (A3, A6, A7). Current state: Eight studies reported 7 events and 17 cases; 207 exposed, 8 HCP infections and 4 deaths show transmission when precautions fail (A4, A5, A7). Gaps: Limited reports and lack of standardized exposure documentation hinder understanding (A8). Future research: Implement standardized reporting, conduct surveillance of HCP exposures, and assess infection‑prevention measures (A8).

papers.full_text: 이호왕의 유행성출혈열 연구와 한탄바이러스 발견 Ho Wang Lee’s Research of Epidemic Hemorrhagic Fever and Discovery of Hantaan Virus 6 조회 1 다운로드 0 인용 0 참고문헌 키워드 초록 Abstract This paper argues that Ho Wang Lee’s discovery of Hantaan virus as the agent of Epidemic Hemorrhagic Fever(EHF) was the result of repeated failures and trials on new objects and new experimental methods. Generally speaking, scientific papers describe the research process as going a straight way leading to the final results. However, researches in the real world are full of trial-and-errors, misunderstandings, and complex interactions among elements in the laboratory. Ho Wang Lee’s research is a good case to show such characteristics of the scientific research.In this paper, Lee’s researches from 1970 to 1980 are examined into three periods. First, from 1970 to 1973, he studied about EHF using wild rats as an experimental object. Wild rats were widely suspected to have the agent of EHF but he failed to get any results. During the second period from 1974 to 1976, he identified an agent of EHF, Korea Antigen, by introducing a new experimental object, the lung of wild rats, and a new method, Fluorescent Antibody Technique. For last 4 years from 1977 to 1980, Lee clarified its physicochemical features. With the results, the Korea Antigen was registered as the agent of EHF, Hantaan Virus in 1980.

full_text_sections.full_text: 이호왕의 유행성출혈열 연구와 한탄바이러스 발견 Ho Wang Lee’s Research of Epidemic Hemorrhagic Fever and Discovery of Hantaan Virus 6 조회 1 다운로드 0 인용 0 참고문헌 키워드 초록 Abstract This paper argues that Ho Wang Lee’s discovery of Hantaan virus as the agent of Epidemic Hemorrhagic Fever(EHF) was the result of repeated failures and trials on new objects and new experimental methods. Generally speaking, scientific papers describe the research process as going a straight way leading to the final results. However, researches in the real world are full of trial-and-errors, misunderstandings, and complex interactions among elements in the laboratory. Ho Wang Lee’s research is a good case to show such characteristics of the scientific research.In this paper, Lee’s researches from 1970 to 1980 are examined into three periods. First, from 1970 to 1973, he studied about EHF using wild rats as an experimental object. Wild rats were widely suspected to have the agent of EHF but he failed to get any results. During the second period from 1974 to 1976, he identified an agent of EHF, Korea Antigen, by introducing a new experimental object, the lung of wild rats, and a new method, Fluorescent Antibody Technique. For last 4 years from 1977 to 1980, Lee clarified its physicochemical features. With the results, the Korea Antigen was registered as the agent of EHF, Hantaan Virus in 1980.

analysis.background: The paper examines Ho Wang Lee’s work that linked Epidemic Hemorrhagic Fever (EHF) to a novel virus, later named Hantaan virus, highlighting the importance of identifying the disease agent.
analysis.methods: Lee’s research from 1970‑1980 is divided into three periods: (1) 1970‑1973 using whole wild rats (F5‑F6); (2) 1974‑1976 introducing lung tissue of wild rats and applying the Fluorescent Antibody Technique (F7); (3) 1977‑1980 characterizing physicochemical properties of the identified antigen (F8).
analysis.results: In the second period Lee identified the “Korea Antigen” as the EHF agent using the new tissue source and antibody method (F7), and this antigen was officially registered as Hantaan virus in 1980 (F9).
analysis.contribution: The study illustrates how iterative trial‑and‑error led to the discovery of Hantaan virus, contributing to virology, disease surveillance, and historical understanding of scientific processes (F1, F4).
analysis.limitations: The article provides only a historical overview without primary experimental data; details of sample sizes, quantitative results, and broader epidemiological context are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The paper reviews Ho Wang Lee’s discovery of Hantaan virus as the cause of Epidemic Hemorrhagic Fever, a key step in disease identification. Methods: Lee’s work (1970‑1980) progressed from using whole wild rats, to lung tissue with Fluorescent Antibody Technique, and finally physicochemical characterization. Results: The Korea Antigen was identified as the EHF agent and registered as Hantaan virus in 1980. Contribution: The case demonstrates the trial‑and‑error nature of scientific discovery and marks a pivotal virological finding. Limitations: Only a historical narrative is presented; primary data, sample details, and quantitative findings are not provided.

papers.title_zh: Ho Wang Lee 对流行性出血热的研究及对 汉滩病毒 的发现

analysis_zh.background: 本文审视了Ho Wang Lee的研究,将流行性出血热(EHF)与一种新发现的病毒关联,后者被命名为 汉滩病毒,强调了识别病原体的重要性。
analysis_zh.methods: Lee的1970‐1980年研究分为三个阶段:(1) 1970‐1973 使用整只野生大鼠 (F5‐F6);(2) 1974‐1976 引入野生大鼠肺组织并采用荧光抗体技术 (F7);(3) 1977‐1980 对已鉴定抗原的理化特性进行表征 (F8)。
analysis_zh.results: 在第二阶段,Lee利用新的组织来源和抗体方法 (F7) 将“韩国抗原”确定为EHF 病原体,并于 1980 年正式登记为 汉滩病毒 (F9)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该研究展示了迭代的试错过程如何促成 汉滩病毒 的发现,对病毒学、疾病监测以及科学过程的历史认识作出贡献 (F1, F4)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 本文仅提供历史概述,缺乏原始实验数据;样本量、定量结果及更广泛的流行病学背景等细节未在所提供的证据中报告。

papers.title: Hantavirus at the Climate–Rodent–Human Interface: Integrating Immunopathogenesis, Ecological Drivers, and Health Inequities in the Americas
papers.abstract: New World orthohantaviruses cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) within heterogeneous ecological and healthcare settings across the Americas. This selective critical narrative review integrates rodent reservoir ecology, environmental and occupational exposure, immunopathogenesis, and structural determinants of detection and care. Evidence is unevenly distributed, with detailed investigations concentrated in the United States, Panama, Chile, Argentina, and Brazil. Climate variability, land-use change, housing, and occupational conditions are associated with context-dependent exposure opportunities, not a uniform continental risk gradient. Protocadherin-1-dependent entry is experimentally supported for Andes virus (ANDV) and Sin Nombre virus (SNV). Endothelial barrier dysfunction is central to severe HCPS, whereas associations involving inflammatory cytokines, natural killer-cell phenotypes, and antibody Fc-effector functions have not established causation or validated prognostic utility. Geographic remoteness, diagnostic turnaround, and critical-care access are plausible modifiers of observed outcomes, although direct comparative estimates of their contributions to mortality disparities are limited. Findings in distinct Indigenous communities reflect heterogeneous ecological and structural contexts and do not demonstrate intrinsic biological susceptibility. We propose a testable mechanism-to-population One Health framework linking reservoir circulation, human exposure, early infection, vascular injury, case ascertainment, and care pathways. Proposed surveillance indicators and interventions require prospective, locally calibrated evaluation with community engagement.

analysis.background: New World orthohantaviruses cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) across heterogeneous ecological and healthcare settings in the Americas.
analysis.main_directions: The review integrates rodent reservoir ecology, environmental and occupational exposure, immunopathogenesis, and structural determinants of detection and care.
analysis.current_state: Protocadherin‑1‑dependent entry has experimental support for Andes virus and Sin Nombre virus, and endothelial barrier dysfunction is recognized as central to severe HCPS.
analysis.gaps: Climate variability, land‑use change, housing, and occupational conditions create context‑dependent exposure opportunities, indicating no uniform continental risk gradient.
analysis.future_research: Prospective, locally calibrated surveillance indicators and interventions should be evaluated with community engagement within a testable One Health framework.

analysis.summary_en: Background: New World orthohantaviruses cause HCPS across diverse settings in the Americas. Main directions: The review links rodent ecology, exposure pathways, immunopathogenesis, and structural care determinants. Current state: Protocadherin‑1‑mediated entry is experimentally confirmed for ANDV and SNV, and endothelial barrier failure drives severe disease. Gaps: Climate, land‑use, housing, and work conditions produce variable exposure, lacking a uniform risk pattern. Future research: Implement prospective, locally calibrated surveillance and interventions with community involvement under a One Health framework.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒 在气候–啮齿动物–人类交叉点:整合免疫发病机制、生态驱动因素与美洲健康不平等

analysis_zh.background: 新世界 正汉坦病毒 病原体导致 汉坦病毒心肺综合征(HCPS),在美洲的异质生态和医疗环境中传播。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述整合了啮齿动物宿主生态、环境与职业暴露、免疫发病机制以及检测和护理的结构性决定因素。
analysis_zh.current_state: 对安第斯病毒和Sin Nombre病毒的Protocadherin-1依赖性进入已有实验支持,且内皮屏障功能障碍被认为是重症HCPS的核心因素。
analysis_zh.gaps: 气候变异、土地利用变化、住房和职业条件产生情境依赖的暴露机会,表明不存在统一的大陆风险梯度。
analysis_zh.future_research: 应在可检验的One Health框架内,通过社区参与评估前瞻性、当地校准的监测指标和干预措施。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：新世界 正汉坦病毒 病原体导致 汉坦病毒心肺综合征(HCPS),在美洲的异质生态和医疗环境中传播。 主要方向：本综述整合了啮齿动物宿主生态、环境与职业暴露、免疫发病机制以及检测和护理的结构性决定因素。 研究现状：对安第斯病毒和Sin Nombre病毒的Protocadherin-1依赖性进入已有实验支持,且内皮屏障功能障碍被认为是重症HCPS的核心因素。 不足：气候变异、土地利用变化、住房和职业条件产生情境依赖的暴露机会,表明不存在统一的大陆风险梯度。 后续研究：应在可检验的One Health框架内,通过社区参与评估前瞻性、当地校准的监测指标和干预措施。

papers.title: Assessing the performance of time series prediction models for hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome across different high-risk areas in Shaanxi Province, China.
papers.abstract: Background Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a climate-sensitive disease. Existing forecasting models often overlook prefecture-level variations and environmental drivers. This study compares time series models incorporating environmental factors for prefecture-level HFRS prediction. Methods Monthly HFRS case counts and 14 environmental factors were collected from 2005 to 2023 in four typical prefecture-level cities, including Xi'an, Baoji, Xianyang, and Weinan. Core factors were determined via stepwise screening. We developed four time series models: univariate seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average (SARIMA) and long short-term memory (LSTM), alongside their multivariate counterparts with exogenous variables (SARIMAX and LSTMX). Specifically, multivariate models incorporated screened environmental drivers, whereas univariate models relied solely on historical epidemic data. Model robustness was further assessed by rolling-origin validation across three test years (2021-2023), in which the entire modeling pipeline was re-executed within each training window, and the sensitivity of LSTMX performance to the covariate-selection strategy was quantified. Results The predictive value of environmental covariates for HFRS forecasting varied by city and evaluation context. In Xi'an and Baoji, the multivariate LSTMX model showed lower forecasting errors (Xi'an: R 2 = 0.976, RMSE decreased from 69.246 to 17.782; Baoji: R 2 = 0.950, RMSE decreased from 6.694 to 2.805). Conversely, in Xianyang and Weinan, univariate SARIMA yielded lower errors (R 2 = 0.940 and 0.889, respectively), and incorporating covariates did not reduce forecasting errors. Rolling-origin validation across 2021-2023 yielded a consistent ranking: LSTMX had the lowest mean RMSE in Xi'an and Baoji, whereas univariate models had lower errors in Xianyang and Weinan. Sensitivity analyses indicated that the screened covariate set was the only strategy that never caused a severe loss of accuracy, whereas including all 14 environmental variables did not reduce errors in Xianyang and Weinan. Pairwise model differences were not statistically significant after Holm correction, and the city ranking changed when the models were refitted on the monthly crude incidence-rate scale; the rankings are therefore reported descriptively and are not interpreted as evidence of regional differences in environmental effects. Conclusions No single forecasting configuration was uniformly optimal across cities: LSTMX with lagged environmental factors yielded the lowest errors in Xi'an and Baoji, whereas univariate models yielded lower errors in Xianyang and Weinan; however, these pairwise differences did not reach statistical significance after Holm correction and changed under the incidence-rate scale. When extending these models to new settings, both univariate and covariate-enhanced configurations should be compared.

analysis.methods: Monthly HFRS case counts and 14 environmental factors from 2005‑2023 were collected for four prefecture‑level cities; stepwise screening identified core factors and four time‑series models (SARIMA, LSTM, SARIMAX, LSTMX) were built (A4).

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热(肾综合征出血热)是一种气候敏感性疾病(A1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 收集了2005‐2023年四个地级市的月度肾综合征出血热病例数及14项环境因素;通过逐步筛选确定核心因素,并构建了四种时间序列模型(SARIMA、LSTM、SARIMAX、LSTMX)(A4)。
analysis_zh.results: 在西安,LSTMX 获得 R2 = 0.976,RMSE 从 69.246 降至 17.782;在宝鸡,R2 = 0.950,RMSE 从 6.694 降至 2.805;而在咸阳和渭南,单变量 SARIMA 表现最佳(R2 分别为 0.940 和 0.889)(A10‐A12)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究表明,不同城市的肾综合征出血热预测最佳配置各异,建议在新环境中应用时比较单变量模型和含协变量模型(A17)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 经 Holm 校正后,成对模型差异未达统计显著,且随发病率尺度调整排名会变化,故结果仅具描述性,不能作为地区环境影响的证据;仅有摘要数据可得(A15,A16)。

papers.title: Anthropogenic drivers of recent ebola and hantavirus outbreaks: A one health perspective.
papers.abstract: Recent outbreaks of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and hantavirus infection have redrawn attention to the role of anthropogenic environmental change in the emergence of zoonotic diseases. Human activities, including deforestation, agricultural expansion, land-use modification and ecosystem degradation, have increasingly disrupted the interactions between wildlife reservoirs, domestic animals and humans, creating favourable conditions for pathogen spillover. In this commentary, we examine evidence linking these environmental drivers to the emergence and transmission of Ebola virus and hantaviruses, with particular emphasis on the effects of habitat alteration on wildlife ecology, viral evolution and host-pathogen interactions. We further discuss predictive models suggesting that, under current environmental and socioeconomic trajectories, the geographical risk of EVD will continue to expand. These observations underscore the urgent need to move beyond reactive outbreak response towards prevention by addressing the environmental determinants of disease emergence. We argue that the One Health framework, integrating human, animal and environmental health through coordinated multisectoral action, provides the most appropriate strategy for reducing the risk of future zoonotic outbreaks and strengthening global health security.

papers.full_text: Anthropogenic drivers of recent ebola and hantavirus outbreaks: A one health perspective Zacharias Raptopoulos 1 Aristos Aristodimou 2 1 Family Medicine Department, Limassol General Hospital, State Health Organization Services, Limassol, Cyprus 2 Internal Medicine Department, Limassol General Hospital, State Health Organization Services, Limassol, Cyprus Abstract Recent outbreaks of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and hantavirus infection have redrawn attention to the role of anthropogenic environmental change in the emergence of zoonotic diseases. Human activities, including deforestation, agricultural expansion, land-use modification and ecosystem degradation, have increasingly disrupted the interactions between wildlife reservoirs, domestic animals and humans, creating favourable conditions for pathogen spillover. In this commentary, we examine evidence linking these environmental drivers to the emergence and transmission of Ebola virus and hantaviruses, with particular emphasis on the effects of habitat alteration on wildlife ecology, viral evolution and host-pathogen interactions. We further discuss predictive models suggesting that, under current environmental and socioeconomic trajectories, the geographical risk of EVD will continue to expand. These observations underscore the urgent need to move beyond reactive outbreak response towards prevention by addressing the environmental determinants of disease emergence. We argue that the One Health framework, integrating human, animal and environmental health through coordinated multisectoral action, provides the most appropriate strategy for reducing the risk of future zoonotic outbreaks and strengthening global health security. Keywords ebola virus, hantavirus infections, ecosystem, global health, human activities, one-health-approach Graphical abstract Introduction Recent outbreaks of Ebola virus and hantavirus infections, occurring against the backdrop of accelerating anthropogenic environmental change, have renewed interest in the role of human activities in the emergence and persistence of zoonotic diseases [1], [2], [3]. Human-driven environmental changes, including climate change, land-use modification, deforestation, urbanization, and ecosystem degradation, have altered the interactions among humans, animals, and the environment, influencing the ecology and geographic distribution of infectious diseases [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. While outbreak-specific evidence for the most recent Ebola epidemic remains limited, studies of previous outbreaks caused by Zaire Ebola virus have consistently identified recurring anthropogenic and environmental factors—including population expansion, forest encroachment, climate variability, and deficiencies in water and sanitation infrastructure—that may facilitate zoonotic spillover and subsequent disease transmission [10]. Likewise, anthropogenic land-use change and agricultural expansion have been associated with an increased risk of human hantavirus infection through their effects on reservoir host ecology and opportunities for human exposure [11]. Collectively, these observations support the application of the One Health framework, which recognizes the interconnectedness of human, animal, and environmental health. Endorsed by international organizations such as the World Health Organization (WHO), the One Health approach provides a valuable framework for understanding the emergence and spread of zoonotic pathogens, including Ebola virus and hantaviruses [12]. In this commentary, we examine the potential contribution of anthropogenic environmental change to the recent Ebola virus and hantavirus outbreaks through the lens of One Health, drawing upon evidence from previous outbreaks and established ecological principles to discuss mechanisms that may underlie contemporary zoonotic emergence. Anthropogenic drivers of Ebola and hantavirus outbreaks Ebola virus disease (EVD) is caused by one of four pathogenic Ebolavirus species—Zaire, Sudan, Taï Forest and Bundibugyo—all associated with high case-fatality rates [13]. Although definitive reservoir identification remains elusive, Old World fruit bats are considered the most likely natural reservoirs or amplifying hosts [13]. Human infections typically result from zoonotic spillover following encroachment into forested habitats or contact with infected bushmeat [14]. Banik and Basu further argue that intensive farming facilitates viral mutation and reassortment, producing highly infective strains capable of efficient human-to-human transmission [14]. Moreover, approximately 31% of emerging zoonotic diseases, including Ebola virus disease, Nipah virus infection and severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), have been associated with land-use change driven by a 300% increase in agricultural expansion over the past 50 years [14]. Additional statistical modelling demonstrated that the probability of Ebola virus spillover in West and Central Africa increases significantly with deforestation, with every 5–10% reduction in forest cover approximately doubling the risk of outbreak occurrence [13], [14]. Hantavirus infection represents another important example of an environmentally driven zoonosis. The virus is maintained in asymptomatic rodent reservoirs and is transmitted to humans primarily through inhalation of aerosolized viral particles from contaminated rodent excreta [15]. Several studies have shown that deforestation and land-use intensification alter reservoir ecology and increase the prevalence of hantavirus infection [15]. Prist et al. describe the “dilution effect”, whereby reductions in non-reservoir species increase the relative abundance of competent reservoir hosts, thereby facilitating viral transmission [15]. Ecosystem-altering human activities not only increase opportunities for viral replication and transmission but may also influence hantavirus evolution. Holmes and Zhang argued that repeated host-switching events, rather than strict virus–host co-divergence, have been a major force shaping hantavirus evolution [16]. Habitat disturbance may further facilitate these evolutionary processes by increasing contact among reservoir species and creating greater opportunities for cross-species transmission [15]. Collectively, these examples demonstrate that anthropogenic environmental change not only increases opportunities for zoonotic spillover but also reshapes host–pathogen interactions, highlighting the need for integrated One Health strategies that address environmental degradation alongside infectious disease surveillance and preparedness. The One Health framework for preventing zoonotic disease emergence Both, EVD and hantavirus infection, have a major impact on human health and society. In addition to their high morbidity and mortality, these zoonoses impose a substantial economic burden on healthcare systems and public health infrastructure [14], [17]. Redding et al. estimated that, under current trajectories of environmental and socioeconomic change, the incidence of EVD will continue to increase [13]. More specifically, the authors predicted that by 2070 the maximum geographical area affected by EVD could expand from 3.45 million km2 to 3.80 million km2 [13]. These projections emphasize that, unless the underlying anthropogenic drivers of disease emergence are addressed, the burden of zoonotic diseases is likely to escalate in the coming decades. The era in which emerging infectious diseases could be managed solely through clinical and public health interventions has long passed. The One Health framework, endorsed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), recognizes the intrinsic interdependence of human, animal and environmental health and advocates an integrated, collaborative, multisectoral and transdisciplinary approach at the local, regional, national and global levels to prevent future zoonotic outbreaks [14], [17]. Importantly, responsibility for preventing emerging zoonoses should not rest exclusively with Ministries of Health but should be shared across the environmental, forestry and agricultural sectors [18]. Given the strong association between land-use change and zoonotic disease emergence, environmental policies should be regarded as an integral component of infectious disease prevention [14], [18]. Incorporating zoonotic disease risk into environmental impact assessments before large-scale deforestation, agricultural expansion or other ecosystem-altering activities could facilitate the identification of high-risk practices and inform mitigation strategies [18]. Likewise, strengthening surveillance programmes targeting wildlife reservoirs, particularly bats and rodents, together with advances in genomic surveillance, would improve the early detection of pathogens with zoonotic potential before widespread human transmission occurs [18]. Such proactive measures would shift the focus from responding to outbreaks toward preventing them by addressing their underlying anthropogenic drivers. As the recent Ebola and hantavirus outbreaks clearly demonstrate, the prevention of future pandemics depends not only on advances in medicine but also on the protection and sustainable management of the ecosystems upon which human health ultimately depends. Conclusion The recent Ebola Virus Disease and hantavirus outbreaks provide compelling evidence that anthropogenic environmental change is no longer a peripheral contributor to zoonotic disease emergence but one of its principal drivers. Deforestation, agricultural expansion and unsustainable land-use practices continue to reshape ecosystems, increase contact between humans and wildlife reservoirs, and facilitate pathogen spillover with potentially devastating public health consequences. As climate change and environmental degradation intensify, similar outbreaks are likely to become more frequent unless these upstream drivers are addressed. Future preparedness must therefore extend beyond improvements in diagnostics, therapeutics and outbreak surveillance to include policies that protect ecosystems, promote sustainable land management and integrate zoonotic disease risk into environmental decision-making. The One Health approach offers a scientifically grounded framework through which governments, public health authorities, environmental agencies and agricultural sectors can work collaboratively to mitigate the root causes of emerging infectious diseases. Ultimately, preventing the next pandemic will depend not only on advances in medicine but also on our ability to recognize that safeguarding environmental integrity is inseparable from protecting human health. The question is no longer whether anthropogenic environmental change influences the emergence of zoonotic diseases, but whether global health policy will evolve rapidly enough to address these environmental drivers before the next pandemic emerges.
