Human-driven environmental changes, including climate change, land-use modification, deforestation, urbanization, and ecosystem degradation, have altered the interactions among humans, animals, and the environment, influencing the ecology and geographic distribution of infectious diseases [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. While outbreak-specific evidence for the most recent Ebola epidemic remains limited, studies of previous outbreaks caused by Zaire Ebola virus have consistently identified recurring anthropogenic and environmental factors—including population expansion, forest encroachment, climate variability, and deficiencies in water and sanitation infrastructure—that may facilitate zoonotic spillover and subsequent disease transmission [10]. Likewise, anthropogenic land-use change and agricultural expansion have been associated with an increased risk of human hantavirus infection through their effects on reservoir host ecology and opportunities for human exposure [11]. Collectively, these observations support the application of the One Health framework, which recognizes the interconnectedness of human, animal, and environmental health. Endorsed by international organizations such as the World Health Organization (WHO), the One Health approach provides a valuable framework for understanding the emergence and spread of zoonotic pathogens, including Ebola virus and hantaviruses [12]. In this commentary, we examine the potential contribution of anthropogenic environmental change to the recent Ebola virus and hantavirus outbreaks through the lens of One Health, drawing upon evidence from previous outbreaks and established ecological principles to discuss mechanisms that may underlie contemporary zoonotic emergence. Anthropogenic drivers of Ebola and hantavirus outbreaks Ebola virus disease (EVD) is caused by one of four pathogenic Ebolavirus species—Zaire, Sudan, Taï Forest and Bundibugyo—all associated with high case-fatality rates [13]. Although definitive reservoir identification remains elusive, Old World fruit bats are considered the most likely natural reservoirs or amplifying hosts [13]. Human infections typically result from zoonotic spillover following encroachment into forested habitats or contact with infected bushmeat [14]. Banik and Basu further argue that intensive farming facilitates viral mutation and reassortment, producing highly infective strains capable of efficient human-to-human transmission [14]. Moreover, approximately 31% of emerging zoonotic diseases, including Ebola virus disease, Nipah virus infection and severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), have been associated with land-use change driven by a 300% increase in agricultural expansion over the past 50 years [14]. Additional statistical modelling demonstrated that the probability of Ebola virus spillover in West and Central Africa increases significantly with deforestation, with every 5–10% reduction in forest cover approximately doubling the risk of outbreak occurrence [13], [14]. Hantavirus infection represents another important example of an environmentally driven zoonosis. The virus is maintained in asymptomatic rodent reservoirs and is transmitted to humans primarily through inhalation of aerosolized viral particles from contaminated rodent excreta [15]. Several studies have shown that deforestation and land-use intensification alter reservoir ecology and increase the prevalence of hantavirus infection [15]. Prist et al. describe the “dilution effect”, whereby reductions in non-reservoir species increase the relative abundance of competent reservoir hosts, thereby facilitating viral transmission [15]. Ecosystem-altering human activities not only increase opportunities for viral replication and transmission but may also influence hantavirus evolution. Holmes and Zhang argued that repeated host-switching events, rather than strict virus–host co-divergence, have been a major force shaping hantavirus evolution [16]. Habitat disturbance may further facilitate these evolutionary processes by increasing contact among reservoir species and creating greater opportunities for cross-species transmission [15]. Collectively, these examples demonstrate that anthropogenic environmental change not only increases opportunities for zoonotic spillover but also reshapes host–pathogen interactions, highlighting the need for integrated One Health strategies that address environmental degradation alongside infectious disease surveillance and preparedness. The One Health framework for preventing zoonotic disease emergence Both, EVD and hantavirus infection, have a major impact on human health and society. In addition to their high morbidity and mortality, these zoonoses impose a substantial economic burden on healthcare systems and public health infrastructure [14], [17]. Redding et al. estimated that, under current trajectories of environmental and socioeconomic change, the incidence of EVD will continue to increase [13]. More specifically, the authors predicted that by 2070 the maximum geographical area affected by EVD could expand from 3.45 million km2 to 3.80 million km2 [13]. These projections emphasize that, unless the underlying anthropogenic drivers of disease emergence are addressed, the burden of zoonotic diseases is likely to escalate in the coming decades. The era in which emerging infectious diseases could be managed solely through clinical and public health interventions has long passed. The One Health framework, endorsed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), recognizes the intrinsic interdependence of human, animal and environmental health and advocates an integrated, collaborative, multisectoral and transdisciplinary approach at the local, regional, national and global levels to prevent future zoonotic outbreaks [14], [17]. analysis_zh.background: 近期埃博拉及汉坦病毒疫情凸显了人为环境变化在动物源性疾病出现中的作用。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 砍伐森林、农业扩张和土地利用改变等人类活动破坏野生动物与人类的接触界面,促进病毒溢出。
analysis_zh.current_state: 证据表明栖息地改变与埃博拉病毒及汉坦病毒传播增加相关,预测模型显示地理风险正扩大。
analysis_zh.gaps: 仍存在对特定宿主动态、环境变化驱动的病毒进化程度以及现有监测有效性的不确定性。
analysis_zh.future_research: 应优先开展综合“一体化健康”监测、环境政策干预以及宿主生态研究,以预防溢出。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：近期埃博拉及汉坦病毒疫情凸显了人为环境变化在动物源性疾病出现中的作用。 主要方向：砍伐森林、农业扩张和土地利用改变等人类活动破坏野生动物与人类的接触界面,促进病毒溢出。 研究现状：证据表明栖息地改变与埃博拉病毒及汉坦病毒传播增加相关,预测模型显示地理风险正扩大。 不足：仍存在对特定宿主动态、环境变化驱动的病毒进化程度以及现有监测有效性的不确定性。 后续研究：应优先开展综合“一体化健康”监测、环境政策干预以及宿主生态研究,以预防溢出。
